ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was preregistered (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/MNUQA will be provided after peer-review) and approved by the university's local ethics committee (#LEK-589).
table.formatted: The study was preregistered (<ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/MNUQA">Link</ref> will be provided after peer-review) and approved by the university's local ethics committee (#LEK-589).

table.text: Clinicians were recruited via the university outpatient clinic and local inpatient clinics with dedicated pain treatment units.

We recruited researchers from this network based on the following two criteria via targeted e-mail invitations: 1) substantial practical and scientific expertise, 2) ensuring representation of different areas of CBT (e.g., third-wave approaches and exposure-based interventions).

Since the expertise indicators including the inclusion criteria were assessed anonymously in the online survey, participants were not excluded from participating in the group Delphi procedure, but their data was excluded before analyses.
All groups followed the same structured procedure: Firstly, informed consent was obtained via an online survey.
In the event of a tie between modules for either the first or second choice, all tied modules were displayed, and participants were asked to rank them.
In the case of science experts, this may in part be explained by selection bias, as two of the four participants reported specific expertise in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Updating the POINT Pain algorithm using a mixed-methods approach
table.research_aims: The research aim of this study is to obtain a matching matrix allocating two CBT interventions to each of 23 questionnaire items. The matching matrix will be developed by a group of clinicians with experience in the treatment of CPP as well as well-known CPP researchers. Regarding the clinicians, a high agreement of > 5 on a 7-point Likert scale is expected. On the researchers’ side, we expect the majority of researchers to agree with the clinicians’ recommendations.
table.research_questions: Which CBT intervention (out of a pre-defined intervention pool containing nine interventions) should be recommended as first choice for a given chronic pain process, and which intervention should be recommended as second choice?
table.study_design_overview:
The study design uses a mixed-methods approach based on focus groups and Delphi technique as well as an online survey. It will be conducted in German (clinicians) and English (researchers). The results will be reported following the recommendations of the Delphi reporting guideline DELPHISTAR (Niederberger et al., 2024).
Recruitment will span two rounds across multiple focus groups: In the first round, licensed CBT therapists as well as therapists in training will be recruited in the university outpatient clinic as well as in regional inpatient clinics with specific pain departments (each handled as separate focus group). All participating therapists receive a short introduction on relevant psychopathological CPP models as well as the CBT interventions included in the matching matrix (table 1). 
After giving their informed consent, participants start an online survey based on the procedure described by Kaiser and Roth (2022), using the German platform SoSciSurvey (Leiner, 2024): We present the participating therapists one treatment target at a time, i. e. a questionnaire item alongside the information that the respective target represents the main problem of a given patient, together with all treatment modules (table 1). The therapists are then asked to drag their intervention of first and second choice to a provided drag-and-drop field. This initial rating will be anonymous and saved.
Following each anonymous recommendation for the respective item, an open discussion is conducted to determine which interventions should be prioritised as the first and second choices. 
In the first focus group, an initial matching matrix will be generated by an open discussion. From the second focus group, the latest matching matrix will be presented as the base for discussion (i. e. the matching matrix based on simple majority, including all data from previous focus groups). The discussion will include one short pro- and con-argument for the presented intervention of first choice, made by participants of the focus group.
After each discussion, participants have the option to change their initial recommendation anonymously in the online survey by being presented the same treatment target again with two drag-and-drop fields alongside all treatment modules (i. e. the second rating). This way, a change of mind as well as the percentage recommending the same intervention can be obtained. The second rating will be used for further analysis as it is deemed to be the more informed decision.
This procedure will be repeated until all 23 items have been discussed. The setting is either online or in person, depending on the capacities of the clinics. Each focus group will have a duration of one and a half to two hours.
As recommended, we aim for five focus groups in the first round (Morgan, 1997, quoted from Vogt et al., 2004, p. 237).  As many inpatient clinics work with multiprofessional teams, all team members will be invited to join the discussion. However, data will only be analysed if sufficient CPP expertise as well as basic knowledge of typical CBT interventions is ensured (see Data Collection Procedures). 
As soon as all groups have been assessed, all participants of all focus groups are invited to the second round that will be conducted as an online survey, using SoSciSurvey (Leiner, 2024). In the second round, participants will be presented the latest matching matrix. For each item-intervention match, participants rate their agreement on a 7-point Likert scale as recommended by Trevelyan and Robinson (2015) (see Measured Variables). Furthermore, an open text-field will be available to leave comments for each item-intervention match.
The final matching matrix will be translated to English and presented to international CPP researchers in a final focus group. They will openly discuss the group discussion’s results and rate their agreement to each recommendation made by the research group on a dichotomous scale (i. e. “recommendation supported” vs. “recommendation not supported”; see Measured Variables). Additionally, opinions regarding Red Flags will be gathered. Results of the open discussion will be noted parallelly. If the agreement of clinicians is ≤ 5 on any given item-intervention match, the researchers’ opinion will be weighted more strongly. Only in that case, if a majority of the researchers votes for another intervention, the intervention will be changed according to their recommendation. Agreement as well as sociodemographic and expertise variables in the researchers’ focus group will be assessed in an anonymous online survey.
table.sampling_and_case_selection_strategy: As no goldstandard for matching specific interventions to specific chronic pain processes exists, we chose this mixed-methods design to obtain recommendations of clinicians with varying degrees of expertise in the treatment of CPP as well of researchers known for their expertise in chronic pain as well as CBT. With this mixed-methods approach, we expect to gain valuable insights with high credibility, as any recommendation will be based on multiple experts' opinions. By using a majority vote, the analysis of each intervention-process match is very transparent and therefore replicable. Through the qualitative data, we additionally gain insights on the reasoning of clinicians as well as researchers when recommending a specific intervention (or choosing not to recommend another).
table.data_source_s_and_data_type_s: We will only use original data: qualitative data gained from open-text fields in the survey as well as notes taken in parallel to the group discussions, quantitative data of the survey regarding majority of recommendations as well as the degree of agreement to any intervention-process match.
table.data_collection_methods:
This is a mixed-methods design based on both the Delphi method as well as focus groups combined with an online survey (see Study Design). 
As expertise in Delphi studies is an issue of ongoing debate (e. g. Baker et al., 2006; Overholser, 2010), we follow recommendations on reporting expertise-relevant variables of the sample (mainly based on Hill et al., 2017, and Overholser, 2010; for researchers Kurniawan et al., 2023) descriptively without making it an in- or exclusion criterion (Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015). This way, we ensure representativeness of the sample (Powell, 2003) regarding the many professions usually involved in the treatment of CPP. However, as a valid matching matrix requires at least some level of experience regarding the treatment of CPP using CBT interventions, data of participants indicating either no CPP treatment experience or no knowledge regarding CBT interventions will be excluded from further analysis.
Anonymity will be ensured by providing an online survey for the initial recommendations as well as giving the opportunity to anonymously change one’s recommendations after the open discussion (Blind & Cuhls, 2001).
Inclusion criteria are: practicing in a German speaking country, basic knowledge of CBT interventions according to self-report (≥ 4 on an 7-point Likert scale), and having treated at least one chronic pain patient (regardless of the setting). Exclusion criteria are: no experience with chronic pain patients, no knowledge of CBT interventions. 
Therapists will be recruited via flyers distributed in the university outpatient clinic as well as contacting regional inpatient clinics with specific pain departments. Researchers will be recruited via e-mail.
table.q9: For all focus groups, an interview guide will be used to ensure a standardised procedure. SoSciSurvey (Leiner, 2024) will be used for the online survey. Notes will be taken in parallel to the group discussion in the researcher focus group using Microsoft Word.

table.stopping_rule:
While consensus is often used as a stopping criterion in Delphi studies, its definition widely varies and it is often confused with agreement (Diamond et al., 2014). Furthermore, consensus does not necessarily reflect the best or even correct outcome (Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015). Therefore, we define the number of focus groups and rounds as stopping criterion instead of consensus: 
The recruitment of the first round will commence either after five focus groups have been conducted or if no further focus groups can be recruited within the timely capacities of this study. 
The second round will take place at the end of February 2025 as soon as all focus groups of the first round have been conducted. There will be no follow-up round after that.
The last focus group with international CPP researchers will take place in the beginning of March 2025. It will be the only round with researchers.
table.data_analysis_approach:
Primary Outcome The primary outcome is the allocation of up to two CBT treatment modules to each of the presented questionnaire items. Of this allocation, a matching matrix will be created based on simple majority.
Secondary Outcome Consensus will be approached using several indicators (Diamond et al., 2014; Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015): First, the agreement to each item-intervention match will be assessed on a 7-point Likert scale (with higher values representing higher agreement) and averaged across the sample. For the researcher Focus Group, agreement will be rated on a dichotomous scale. Additionally, the percentage of participants recommending the same intervention will be computed both pre- and post-discussion. Variability in the recommendations across the sample as well as the stability of recommendations pre- to post-discussion will be analysed, serving as an estimate for reliability.

A matching matrix will be generated allocating two interventions to each item of a questionnaire according to the most frequently chosen interventions of the second rating in the first round of focus groups. The hierarchical order of the interventions (in first and second choice) results directly from the interventions selected by the majority in the respective position.
The agreement will be averaged across the whole sample for each item-intervention match and reported as mean and standard deviation. For the researcher group, agreement will be descriptively reported as frequencies. The percentage of participants with the same recommendation will be reported descriptively as well as depicted graphically. Likewise, the stability of recommendations will be depicted graphically (e. g. in a matrix). A statistical analysis of stability will not be executed because of the nominal structure of the dependent variable (i. e. CBT interventions).
Also because of the nominal-scaled CBT interventions, variance in the recommendations cannot be analysed using the usual parameters. Therefore, measures like the Gibbs-Martin Index will be separately computed for the first and second choice as well as before and after the discussion (Gibbs & Martin, 1962). Scores will be reported descriptively. The difference between the pre- and post-discussion scores will be computed. A low Gibbs-Martin Index score indicates low variance in the sample’s recommendations, thus supporting higher consensus.  
Data of participants who do either not fulfil all inclusion criteria or fulfil at least one exclusion criterion will be excluded from analysis. 
All available data will be analysed, as long as no data exclusion criteria (see above) apply. 
If applicable, subgroups (e. g. participants with more or less job experience, older or younger participants etc.) will be compared regarding their recommendations and agreement to the final matching matrix.
table.data_analysis_process: The study management as well as research assistants will be involved in the data analysis. Quantitative data will be analysed using the statistic software RStudio (RStudio Team (2020). RStudio: Integrated Development for R. RStudio, PBC, Boston, MA URL http://www.rstudio.com/).
table.credibility_strategies: Bringing in different perspectives Consensus building among team members or 'interrater reliability'
table.q14: Despite the qualitative approach of this study, the main outcome is quantitative in nature. By bringing in different perspectives (clincians with varying degrees of experience, researchers), the data is expected to be robust and representative. It is not planned to rate the qualitative data, but rather to inform the interpretation of the quantitative results be retracing the reasoning of the study participants. Consensus is aimed from already with the study participants.

#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: The study was preregistered (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/MNUQA will be provided after peer-review) and approved by the university's local ethics committee (#LEK-589).
live_data_statements: Clinicians were recruited via the university outpatient clinic and local inpatient clinics with dedicated pain treatment units.

We recruited researchers from this network based on the following two criteria via targeted e-mail invitations: 1) substantial practical and scientific expertise, 2) ensuring representation of different areas of CBT (e.g., third-wave approaches and exposure-based interventions).

Since the expertise indicators including the inclusion criteria were assessed anonymously in the online survey, participants were not excluded from participating in the group Delphi procedure, but their data was excluded before analyses.
All groups followed the same structured procedure: Firstly, informed consent was obtained via an online survey.
In the event of a tie between modules for either the first or second choice, all tied modules were displayed, and participants were asked to rank them.
In the case of science experts, this may in part be explained by selection bias, as two of the four participants reported specific expertise in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:3, File = c("Analyses_phase 1.Rmd", 
"Analyses_phase 2.Rmd", "Analyses_phase 3.Rmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", "numeric")), row.names = c(NA, 
-3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**4 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `Phase_2.xlsx` to `../Data/Datasets/Phase_2.xlsx` (in Analyses_phase 2.Rmd); `Phase_1.xlsx` to `../Data/Datasets/Phase_1.xlsx` (in Analyses_phase 2.Rmd); `Phase_3.xlsx` to `../Data/Datasets/Phase_3.xlsx` (in Analyses_phase 3.Rmd); `Phase_1.xlsx` to `../Data/Datasets/Phase_1.xlsx` (in Analyses_phase 1.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 0 ran without error, 3 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.
**Undefined-variable errors**

**3 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Analyses_phase 1.Rmd", "Analyses_phase 2.Rmd", 
"Analyses_phase 3.Rmd"), "Missing variable" = c("ds", "ds", "ds_clean"
), "Defined in" = c("(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)", 
"(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)", "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"
)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

reproducibility_check.checklist_section: We ran the paper's 3 R scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. 3 identical copies of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, were not run again. **0 of 3 scripts ran to the end**: 3 stopped with an error. | Script | Result | What happened | |---|---|---| | Analyses_phase 1.Rmd | Stopped with an error | Error in eval(e, envir = env) : object 'ds' not found | | Analyses_phase 2.Rmd | Stopped with an error | Error in eval(e, envir = env) : object 'ds' not found | | Analyses_phase 3.Rmd | Stopped with an error | Error in eval(e, envir = env) : object 'ds_clean' not found | ### How to make your code run on another computer We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it. **A script uses something it does not create or load itself.** - Analyses_phase 1.Rmd: ds - Analyses_phase 2.Rmd: ds - Analyses_phase 3.Rmd: ds_clean Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it. 1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R). 2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing. 3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second. 4. Load every package with library() at the top. ### Comparison with the paper We found no statistical tests in the paper to compare with the output of the code.

text.text: View-only link to data and analysis scripts: https://osf.io/mky3c/overview?view_only=06f4c3ae6cbd4f9ea8e1864a793aa3a3 Supplements can be provided upon request and will otherwise be published with the peerreviewed manuscript.
text.formatted: View-only link to data and analysis scripts: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/mky3c/overview?view_only=06f4c3ae6cbd4f9ea8e1864a793aa3a3">https://osf.io/mky3c/overview?view_only=06f4c3ae6cbd4f9ea8e1864a793aa3a3</ref> Supplements can be provided upon request and will otherwise be published with the peerreviewed manuscript.

text.text: Chronic pain is a highly prevalent (Calvo et al., 2025) as well as heterogeneous condition, requiring interdisciplinary and multimodal treatment approaches (Breivik et al., 2006; Cohen et al., 2021; Sundström et al., 2025; Turk, 1990).
text.formatted: Chronic pain is a highly prevalent <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Calvo et al., 2025)</ref> as well as heterogeneous condition, requiring interdisciplinary and multimodal treatment approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Breivik et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cohen et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Sundström et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Turk, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Among psychological treatments, cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) are recommended by multiple guidelines (Becker & Straßner, 2023; National Institute for Health and Care Excellence [NICE], 2021).
text.formatted: Among psychological treatments, cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) are recommended by multiple guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Becker & Straßner, 2023</ref>; National Institute for Health and Care Excellence [NICE], 2021).

text.text: However, treatment effects at the group level remain moderate (Vlaeyen & Crombez, 2020; Williams et al., 2020), and even seemed to become smaller with improving meta-analytic methods (McCracken, 2023).
text.formatted: However, treatment effects at the group level remain moderate <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Vlaeyen & Crombez, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Williams et al., 2020)</ref>, and even seemed to become smaller with improving meta-analytic methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(McCracken, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Given the heterogeneity of chronic pain syndromes and the substantial variability in individual treatment responses (McCracken & Turk, 2002; Scholten et al., 2025), it is plausible that nomothetic, group-based research might not adequately capture individual treatment effects (Gloster et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Given the heterogeneity of chronic pain syndromes and the substantial variability in individual treatment responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(McCracken & Turk, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Scholten et al., 2025)</ref>, it is plausible that nomothetic, group-based research might not adequately capture individual treatment effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Gloster et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This heterogeneity encompasses comorbidities (e.g., Desai et al., 2020), previous and ongoing treatments, functional limitations, and psychosocial circumstances ('Guiding Principles', 2023).
text.formatted: This heterogeneity encompasses comorbidities (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Desai et al., 2020)</ref>, previous and ongoing treatments, functional limitations, and psychosocial circumstances <ref type="bibr">('Guiding Principles', 2023)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, the availability of high-quality treatment and specialised clinicians is often limited and waiting time for a treatment can be from months to over a year, depending on the country of residence or region (e.g. Baker et al., 2024; Grant et al., 2023; Purcell et al., 2022).
text.formatted: At the same time, the availability of high-quality treatment and specialised clinicians is often limited and waiting time for a treatment can be from months to over a year, depending on the country of residence or region (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Baker et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Grant et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Purcell et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In line with a biopsychosocial understanding of chronic pain and to address these challenges, personalised treatment and research approaches targeting disabilitymaintaining processes targetable in therapy are increasingly advocated (Bartels et al., 2022; Finan & Garland, 2015; McCracken, 2023; Murillo et al., 2022; Scholten et al., 2025; Turk, 1990; Vlaeyen & Morley, 2005).
text.formatted: In line with a biopsychosocial understanding of chronic pain and to address these challenges, personalised treatment and research approaches targeting disabilitymaintaining processes targetable in therapy are increasingly advocated <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bartels et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Finan & Garland, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">McCracken, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Murillo et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Scholten et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Turk, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Vlaeyen & Morley, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: These efforts require clear clinical recommendations to enable evidence-based personalised treatment.
The terms "processes of change" and "mechanisms of change" are often used interchangeably.

While mechanisms of change are commonly defined as mediating pathways that explain how an intervention leads to changes in outcomes (Ehring et al., 2022; Kazdin, 2007), Hayes and colleagues conceptualize processes of change more broadly as dynamic, potentially non-linear phenomena that may operate across multiple levels of analysis (Hayes et al., 2020).
text.formatted: While mechanisms of change are commonly defined as mediating pathways that explain how an intervention leads to changes in outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Ehring et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Kazdin, 2007)</ref>, Hayes and colleagues conceptualize processes of change more broadly as dynamic, potentially non-linear phenomena that may operate across multiple levels of analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Hayes et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, processes of change should be theory-based and modifiable.
However, while this framework specifies characteristics that processes should exhibit, it does not provide a clearly delineated set of processes themselves.

In the present study, processes were derived from established psychological models of chronic pain (Scholten & Glombiewski, 2024), for example avoidance behaviour as described in the fear-avoidance model (Vlaeyen et al., 2016).
text.formatted: In the present study, processes were derived from established psychological models of chronic pain <ref type="bibr">(Scholten & Glombiewski, 2024)</ref>, for example avoidance behaviour as described in the fear-avoidance model <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Vlaeyen et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, the processes used in this study are theory-derived constructs that have been proposed to contribute to the maintenance of pain-related disability and other burdensome pain-related experiences.
These processes are not assumed to represent isolated causal mechanisms but are used to derive clinically meaningful treatment targets for personalised intervention selection.

Thus, we use the term process when referring to general psychological processes and their assessment, while the term treatment target denotes a specific process selected in the context of treatment and clinical decision-making.
All treatment targets are therefore process-based.

More specifically, treatment targets represent clinically actionable manifestations of broader psychological processes, for example asking others to take over a strenuous task (target) as a specific manifestation of avoidance behaviour (process).
The specific processes are listed in the Study Materials section and the individual targets are summarised in Table 2.
text.formatted: The specific processes are listed in the Study Materials section and the individual targets are summarised in Table <ref type="table">2</ref>.

text.text: Following our previous definition (Reference), an intervention is embedded within a treatment module that provides structure to its implementation, including preparation, execution, and consolidation.
A treatment module extends beyond the isolated delivery of an intervention.

For example, exposure in vivo may involve preparatory elements that establish treatment rationale and commitment (e.g., creating a movement hierarchy), the intervention itself (e.g., behavioural exposure), and procedures intended to consolidate treatment effects (e.g., self-management goals).
To link treatment modules to predefined treatment targets in a transparent and reproducible manner, a Matching Matrix is required.
A Matching Matrix therefore does not encompass the full clinical decision-making process and does not determine which treatment target should be prioritised.
Rather, it supports the selection of a treatment module once a target has been identified.
In contrast, an algorithm encompasses the broader clinical decisionmaking process, including both target selection and treatment module indication (Reference).
In routine clinical practice, therapists already personalise treatment because recommendations derived from nomothetic averages frequently do not fit individual patients (Levinson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In routine clinical practice, therapists already personalise treatment because recommendations derived from nomothetic averages frequently do not fit individual patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Levinson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: CBT therapists therefore rely on case conceptualisations and flexible adaptations of treatment protocols -an approach that calls the utility of protocols into question (McCracken, 2023).
text.formatted: CBT therapists therefore rely on case conceptualisations and flexible adaptations of treatment protocols -an approach that calls the utility of protocols into question <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(McCracken, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, clinical judgments underlying case conceptualisations are prone to cognitive biases and limited reliability (Lutz et al., 2022; Scholten et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Moreover, clinical judgments underlying case conceptualisations are prone to cognitive biases and limited reliability <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Lutz et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Scholten et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Modular treatment frameworks, such as the Unified Protocol for emotional disorders (Barlow et al., 2017), offer an alternative to rigid protocols.
text.formatted: Modular treatment frameworks, such as the Unified Protocol for emotional disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Barlow et al., 2017)</ref>, offer an alternative to rigid protocols.

text.text: Process-based therapy has been proposed as an advancement to evidence-based practice in order to directly address processes of change instead of mere symptoms (Hofmann & Hayes, 2019).
text.formatted: Process-based therapy has been proposed as an advancement to evidence-based practice in order to directly address processes of change instead of mere symptoms <ref type="bibr">(Hofmann & Hayes, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, evidence is not yet sufficient to delineate process-intervention matches.

In parallel, data-informed decision-support systems that integrate clinical expertise into their statistical models have been proposed to address limitations of intuitive clinical judgement (Burger et al., 2022; Levinson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In parallel, data-informed decision-support systems that integrate clinical expertise into their statistical models have been proposed to address limitations of intuitive clinical judgement <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Burger et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Levinson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Across psychotherapy research, support-tools have been developed to match interventions to targets (e.g. Fernandez et al., 2017; Kaiser & Roth, 2022; Rubel et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Across psychotherapy research, support-tools have been developed to match interventions to targets (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Fernandez et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Kaiser & Roth, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Rubel et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For mood and anxiety disorders, the algorithm developed by Fernandez and colleagues (2017) demonstrated promising effects (Fisher et al., 2019).
text.formatted: For mood and anxiety disorders, the algorithm developed by <ref type="bibr">Fernandez and colleagues (2017)</ref> demonstrated promising effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Fisher et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, evidence for the superiority of such algorithms over usual clinical decision-making remains scarce.
Crucially, such approaches presuppose clearly specified links between interventions and the psychological processes they are intended to change.
In the absence of structured and empirically grounded target-intervention mappings, decision-support systems risk reproducing intuitive or heuristic decision-making rather than improving upon it.

Idiographic and process-focused approaches have been proposed across clinical domains to complement nomothetic models by emphasising within-person change and mechanism-based decision-making (Fisher & Boswell, 2016; Levinson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Idiographic and process-focused approaches have been proposed across clinical domains to complement nomothetic models by emphasising within-person change and mechanism-based decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Fisher & Boswell, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Levinson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such approaches have shown promise in other heterogeneous conditions, including depression (Fisher et al., 2019) and eating disorders (Levinson et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Such approaches have shown promise in other heterogeneous conditions, including depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Fisher et al., 2019)</ref> and eating disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Levinson et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Both studies underscore the need for frameworks that systematically link interventions to treatment targets.
In chronic pain research, structured approaches to matching interventions to treatment targets remain particularly underdeveloped (Mauck et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In chronic pain research, structured approaches to matching interventions to treatment targets remain particularly underdeveloped <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Mauck et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Existing personalisation strategies in chronic pain illustrate this limitation in different ways.

Stratified care models assign patients to different treatment intensities based on group-level risk profiles (Scholten & Glombiewski, 2024) and have shown modest benefits in low back pain (Foster et al., 2014; Hill et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Stratified care models assign patients to different treatment intensities based on group-level risk profiles <ref type="bibr">(Scholten & Glombiewski, 2024)</ref> and have shown modest benefits in low back pain <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Foster et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Hill et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: However, recent meta-analytic evidence suggests limited advantages over usual care (Chiodo & Haley, 2024).
text.formatted: However, recent meta-analytic evidence suggests limited advantages over usual care <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Chiodo & Haley, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, stratified approaches do not specify how particular interventions affect individual processes.

More highly personalised treatments for chronic pain, often based on patients' preferences, have also shown encouraging results (Åsenlöf et al., 2005 , 2009; Evers et al., 2002; Ferwerda et al., 2017; Gasslander et al., 2022; Kerns et al., 2014; van Koulil et al., 2010).
text.formatted: More highly personalised treatments for chronic pain, often based on patients' preferences, have also shown encouraging results <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Åsenlöf et al., 2005</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Evers et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Ferwerda et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Gasslander et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Kerns et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">van Koulil et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, preference-based personalisation remains vulnerable to bias and does not ensure that selected interventions are optimally aligned with the most relevant treatment targets for a given individual.

Robust moderators of treatment effects have yet to be identified in chronic pain research (Murillo et al., 2022), while traditional mediation and moderation models may be ill-suited to capture complex, non-linear, and reciprocal processes (Hayes et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Robust moderators of treatment effects have yet to be identified in chronic pain research <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Murillo et al., 2022)</ref>, while traditional mediation and moderation models may be ill-suited to capture complex, non-linear, and reciprocal processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Hayes et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, this raises several key questions for personalised psychotherapy: In the absence of a comprehensive empirical evidence base, how can personalised treatment decisions be improved?
Which psychological processes should be assessed, which interventions are best suited to address them, and how should interventions be systematically matched to treatment targets?
One approach to addressing the gap between intuitive and data-based decision-making is the systematic involvement of clinicians in the development of decision-support tools.

In other clinical contexts, expert-informed approaches have been used to formalise interventiontarget relationships and guide treatment selection (Bartels et al., 2022; Burger et al., 2022; Kaiser & Roth, 2022; Mauck et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In other clinical contexts, expert-informed approaches have been used to formalise interventiontarget relationships and guide treatment selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bartels et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Burger et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Kaiser & Roth, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Mauck et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Involving science experts may further help bridge the science-practice gap.

The present study therefore aimed to develop a Matching Matrix, that is, a structured framework linking psychological chronic pain-related processes to the two CBT modules expected to target them most effectively, using a group Delphi approach to establish high agreement among experts (Niederberger et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The present study therefore aimed to develop a Matching Matrix, that is, a structured framework linking psychological chronic pain-related processes to the two CBT modules expected to target them most effectively, using a group Delphi approach to establish high agreement among experts <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Niederberger et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Informed consent as well as all data were assessed online using the platform SoSci Survey (Leiner, 2024).
text.formatted: Informed consent as well as all data were assessed online using the platform SoSci Survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Leiner, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Patients as well as the general public have not been involved in the study's conceptualisation.
Reporting standards are provided in the Appendix (A) using the DELPHISTAR protocol (Niederberger et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Reporting standards are provided in the Appendix (A) using the DELPHISTAR protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Niederberger et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The aim of the present study was to develop a Matching Matrix assigning two CBT modules ("first choice" and "second choice") to 23 treatment targets (i. e. items assessing facets of chronic pain processes, see Study Materials).
To bridge the science-practice gap and bring in multiple perspectives, the development process was designed to take place in close collaboration with clinicians as well as science experts.
For this purpose, the Delphi technique represents a suitable method.

The Delphi technique is used to survey experts in the field, usually across multiple rounds, in order to facilitate the development of consensus, or at a minimum increase agreement (Boulkedid et al., 2011; Niederberger et al., 2024; Powell, 2003; Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015).
text.formatted: The Delphi technique is used to survey experts in the field, usually across multiple rounds, in order to facilitate the development of consensus, or at a minimum increase agreement <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Boulkedid et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Niederberger et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Powell, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, consensus does not necessarily lead to the best or "correct" results (Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015).
text.formatted: However, consensus does not necessarily lead to the best or "correct" results <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, when consensus develops across repeated rounds, it cannot be ruled out that this reflects normative processes, such as conformity pressure, rather than convergence towards the most well-supported judgment (Powell, 2003).
text.formatted: Moreover, when consensus develops across repeated rounds, it cannot be ruled out that this reflects normative processes, such as conformity pressure, rather than convergence towards the most well-supported judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Powell, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Consensus has also been criticised as a stopping criterion because it is inconsistently defined and reported across Delphi studies (Diamond et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Consensus has also been criticised as a stopping criterion because it is inconsistently defined and reported across Delphi studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Diamond et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Against this background, the following approach was implemented in the present study: A group Delphi approach was adopted, whereby separate groups of clinicians were invited to openly discuss and provide anonymous responses to an online survey (Niederberger et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Against this background, the following approach was implemented in the present study: A group Delphi approach was adopted, whereby separate groups of clinicians were invited to openly discuss and provide anonymous responses to an online survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Niederberger et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Following common recommendations, the number of Delphi rounds was set a priori to two (Diamond et al., 2014; Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015), resulting in Study Phases 1 and 2.
text.formatted: Following common recommendations, the number of Delphi rounds was set a priori to two <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Diamond et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015)</ref>, resulting in Study Phases 1 and 2.

text.text: In Study Phase 3, a focus group was conducted with science experts to review the results of the Delphi groups.
For each phase, a selection criterion was defined a priori.
These criteria were intended to identify promising treatment-target matches for further investigation rather than to establish definitive consensus or empirically validated treatment recommendations.
The specific criteria are described below along with the associated study phases.
Variability in responses was assessed in Phase 1 to characterise the distribution of expert judgments (see Analyses) (Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015).
text.formatted: Variability in responses was assessed in Phase 1 to characterise the distribution of expert judgments (see Analyses) <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than using consensus as a stopping criterion, agreement was used to operationalise the extent to which a treatment module was consistently recommended for a given psychological process.
For study phases 1 and 2, clinicians from inpatient and outpatient settings were included.
As recommended (Vogt et al., 2004), we aimed to conduct five groups, with an overall target sample size of n = 25.
text.formatted: As recommended <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Vogt et al., 2004)</ref>, we aimed to conduct five groups, with an overall target sample size of n = 25.

text.text: Clinicians were recruited via the university outpatient clinic and local inpatient clinics with dedicated pain treatment units.
In inpatient clinics, the whole practitioner team was invited to participate, therefore different professions are represented.
Only participants who agreed to be contacted again in phase 1 were invited to the second Delphi round (phase 2).
For the science expert focus group (phase 3), we aimed for a sample size of n = 5.
Science experts were identified through an academic network supported by the Research Foundation -Flanders (FWO, Research Community PAIN).

We recruited researchers from this network based on the following two criteria via targeted e-mail invitations: 1) substantial practical and scientific expertise, 2) ensuring representation of different areas of CBT (e.g., third-wave approaches and exposure-based interventions).
Knowledge of CBT interventions and having treated at least one chronic pain patient were defined as inclusion criteria for both science and clinical experts.

These criteria allowed the inclusion of different professions and levels of experience, consistent with the recommendation of recruiting heterogeneous samples for Delphi studies to enhance the validity of the results (Baker et al., 2006), whilst ensuring the necessary knowledge to match CBT interventions to specific treatment targets.
text.formatted: These criteria allowed the inclusion of different professions and levels of experience, consistent with the recommendation of recruiting heterogeneous samples for Delphi studies to enhance the validity of the results <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baker et al., 2006)</ref>, whilst ensuring the necessary knowledge to match CBT interventions to specific treatment targets.

text.text: CBT knowledge was assessed on a 7-point scale (1 = no knowledge,7 = in-depth knowledge).
Participants who indicated knowledge below 4 ("basic knowledge") were excluded from analyses.

Since the expertise indicators including the inclusion criteria were assessed anonymously in the online survey, participants were not excluded from participating in the group Delphi procedure, but their data was excluded before analyses.
The conducting researcher (first author) did not observe a negative influence of excluded participants on the discussion process.
In Delphi studies, expertise is usually used as an inclusion criterion (Powell, 2003; Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015).
text.formatted: In Delphi studies, expertise is usually used as an inclusion criterion <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Powell, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, the concept of expertise remains poorly defined (Baker et al., 2006).
text.formatted: However, the concept of expertise remains poorly defined <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baker et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than operationalising expertise through predefined eligibility criteria, relevant indicators for clinical and scientific expertise were retrieved from relevant literature (Baker et al., 2006; Hill et al., 2017; Kurniawan et al., 2023; Overholser, 2010), assessed via self-report, and will be reported in detail in the sample description, in accordance with recommendations (Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015).
text.formatted: Rather than operationalising expertise through predefined eligibility criteria, relevant indicators for clinical and scientific expertise were retrieved from relevant literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baker et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Hill et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Kurniawan et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Overholser, 2010)</ref>, assessed via self-report, and will be reported in detail in the sample description, in accordance with recommendations <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015</ref>).

text.text: These indicators for example included years of professional experience, number of treated chronic pain patients, or self-ratings of empathic skills for clinicians, and taking part in national and international collaborations and self-rated communication skills for science experts.
The complete study procedure is summarised in Figure 1.
text.formatted: The complete study procedure is summarised in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: All assessments took place between January and March 2025.
The aim of phase 1 was to develop an initial Matching Matrix based on clinicians' recommendations.
As selection criterion, a majority of clinicians (> 50 %) recommending the same module for the same treatment target was set.
text.formatted: As selection criterion, a majority of clinicians (> 50 %) recommending the same module for the same treatment target was set.

text.text: Phase 1 represents the first Delphi round and was conducted in separate groups to develop an initial Matching Matrix based on clinicians' recommendations.
Discussions were conducted separately in five groups, with each round building iteratively on the previous one.
All groups were conducted and moderated by the first author (first author), a female licensed psychotherapist (CBT) employed at the university as a PhD student.

She did not partake in the open discussion, but kept track of time, answered questions regarding targets or modules, and moderated the discussion ensuring that all participants felt comfortable to speak.
She also ensured that the discussion remained on the topic and ensured that arguments were not based on misunderstandings or incorrect information.
In two groups, participating clinicians worked at the university outpatient clinic, therefore knowing the conducting researcher (first author).
Otherwise there was no personal contact between the conducting researcher and participants prior to or after conduction.
Licensed psychotherapists and physicians received continuing education credits for their participation.
The discussions were not recorded.
Each group took between 60 and 90 minutes.
Face-to-face groups took place in the university outpatient clinic and local inpatient clinics, online groups were conducted via the platform Zoom (https://www.zoom.com/).
text.formatted: Face-to-face groups took place in the university outpatient clinic and local inpatient clinics, online groups were conducted via the platform Zoom (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zoom.com/">https://www.zoom.com/</ref>).

text.text: The format of the groups depended on the capacities of the clinics and the interviewer.
Only participating clinicians and the conducting researcher were present during conduction.
All groups followed the same structured procedure: Firstly, informed consent was obtained via an online survey.
This survey followed the approach described by Kaiser and Roth (2022) and allowed for anonymous responses.
text.formatted: This survey followed the approach described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Kaiser and Roth (2022)</ref> and allowed for anonymous responses.

text.text: The clinicians were informed regarding the affiliation of the conducting researcher as well as the aim of the study project.
Second, sociodemographic data and self-reported expertise indicators were assessed in the online survey.

Third, each item of the ProCEss item set, a German item set assessing various psychological processes related to chronic pain (see Study Materials) (references), was presented and the clinicians were asked to select their first and second choice CBT module for each item.
The clinicians were instructed to imagine a patient presenting for an initial assessment session whose most promising target process was represented by the item currently displayed.
For positively worded items (e. g. self-efficacy), the clinicians were asked to imagine a patient with low scores, with the therapeutic goal being to strengthen this process.
This first rating was made anonymously in the survey.
Fourth, in the first group, the clinicians were instructed to discuss their selections.
From the second group, the two most frequently selected modules per item were presented.
The clinicians were invited to provide arguments in favour of as well as against the presented module choices and could suggest and justify other options.
Fifth, clinicians provided a second rating that was later used for analyses as it was considered to reflect the more informed decision.
The aim of phase 2 was to assess the agreement of the clinicians with the Matching Matrix developed based on phase 1.
As selection criterion, a mean agreement of >5 on a 7point scale (0 = do not agree at all,6 = completely agree) for each target-module match was set.
text.formatted: As selection criterion, a mean agreement of >5 on a 7point scale (0 = do not agree at all,6 = completely agree) for each target-module match was set.

text.text: Phase 2 represents the second Delphi round.
It was conducted online and could be completed by clinicians over a period of two weeks.
Study information was provided in written form with the invitation email as well as in the online survey to download.
The clinicians gave their informed consent in the online survey.
After providing sociodemographic and expertise information, the clinicians were presented with the results of phase 1 one match at a time.
If the same module had been selected most frequently as both first and second choice, the next most frequently selected module was presented as the second option.
In the event of a tie between modules for either the first or second choice, all tied modules were displayed, and participants were asked to rank them.
They also had the option to provide written comments.
These qualitative comments were used in cases that did not meet the pre-defined selection criteria to complete the matching matrix.
The aim of phase 3 was to review the clinicians' selections by a focus group with psychological science experts.
The primary criterion for final module selection in this group was majority agreement (> 50%) for each target-module match.
text.formatted: The primary criterion for final module selection in this group was majority agreement (> 50%) for each target-module match.

text.text: If no clear majority emerged for a given target in Phase 1, the decision could be overruled by the focus group of science experts.
That means, a module was considered accepted if a majority was reached either among the clinicians or among the science experts, or among both.
Since the science experts were not participating in the previous phases, this phase was not considered another Delphi round.
This rationale provided clear decision rules in the case of unfulfilled majority criteria in Phases 1 and 3.
Study information was provided in written form via email prior to the session.
All science experts gave verbal consent to the recording of the discussion.
The science experts received the same theoretical introduction as the clinicians in phase 1.
Recording began after this introduction, when the science experts were presented with the results of the clinicians' ratings of phase 1.
They were invited to discuss potential contraindications for the selected modules and to specify under which conditions the secondchoice module might be preferable to the first-choice module.
The recorded discussion was transcribed by a research assistant also present in the meeting for qualitative assessment of the discussion.
The transcript was not returned to the participants.
The qualitative comments transcribed were used in cases that did not meet the pre-defined selection criteria to complete the matching matrix.

Following the discussion of each target-module match, science experts completed an online survey in which they indicated their agreement with each target-module match on a dichotomous scale (agreement vs. disagreement), regardless of the position of the module as first or second choice.
They also provided sociodemographic and self-assessed expertise indicators (see Study Materials).
The science experts' focus group took 90 minutes.

The set of potential targets was based on the German "Prozesse Chronischer Schmerzen ErfaSSen" (ProCEss; English: "Assessing chronic pain processes") item set.

Within this item set, psychological processes were selected based on established psychological models of chronic pain (e.g. the Fear-Avoidance model ( Vlaeyen et al., 2016))as well as the IMMPACT recommendations of important pain experience variables (Dworkin et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Within this item set, psychological processes were selected based on established psychological models of chronic pain (e.g. the Fear-Avoidance model ( <ref type="formula">Vlaeyen et al., 2016))</ref>as well as the IMMPACT recommendations of important pain experience variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dworkin et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: The ProCEss item set is theory-driven, based on psychological models of chronic pain, and has been qualitatively validated in German language (Reference) and demonstrates overall sufficient psychometric properties in the German version (Reference).

Of the ProCEss item set, 23 items assessing specific manifestations of the processes catastrophising, avoidance behaviour, depressive symptoms, acceptance, values-based action, expectations, thought suppression, task persistency, positive affect, negative affect, selfefficacy, and self-compassion, were used in this study (for items, also see Table 2).

text.text: The treatment modules were selected to represent conceptually distinct strategies that could be evaluated individually within the matching framework.

Consequently, interventions that were considered to reflect overarching therapeutic skills, e.g. mindfulness, were not included as separate modules, as they are considered to be embedded within several modules, e.g. attention regulation and acceptance-based interventions.

The majority of clinicians recommending the same module (selection criterion of phase 1) was calculated as frequencies with which each module was recommended per target after group discussion.
As preregistered, the Gibbs-Martin Index was calculated to quantify variability in clinicians' selections (Gibbs & Martin, 1962).
text.formatted: As preregistered, the Gibbs-Martin Index was calculated to quantify variability in clinicians' selections <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Gibbs & Martin, 1962)</ref>.

text.text: Given that participants could choose from nine predefined CBT modules, the index could range from 0 to 0.89.
The closer the index is to 0, the fewer categories are selected -indicating a clearer consensus.
Conversely, values approaching the upper limit suggest more evenly distributed selections across modules, reflecting lower agreement.

The index was calculated across all item-module matches for the first and second rating and separately for the first and second choices, resulting in four indices (first rating -first choices, first rating -second choices, second rating -first choices, second rating -second choices).
Qualitative comments of phases 2 and 3 were only used if the predefined selection criteria were not met.
If necessary, the qualitative comments were reviewed by the study team.

The study team consisted of three female psychologists, one licensed psychotherapist and PhD (co-author), one licensed psychotherapist and PhD student (first author), and one psychotherapist in training and PhD student.
Qualitative comments were reviewed descriptively rather than analysed using a formal qualitative methodology.
Their purpose was to identify alternative module recommendations and to better understand reasons underlying disagreement with the proposed recommendations from phase 1.
Information retrieved from the qualitative comments complemented the recommendation frequencies of phase 1 that were also reviewed in cases of unmet selection criteria.
In the first Delphi round (phase 1), n = 25 clinicians participated in five focus groups.
Three clinicians were excluded from the final analyses: two participants reported no prior treatment experience with chronic pain patients, and one rated their CBT knowledge below "basic knowledge".
This resulted in a final sample size of n = 22.
The sociodemographic and expertise characteristics of all three samples are summarised in Table 1.

For the first 23 first-choice selections, 66.40 % of recommendations met the criterion of a simple majority.
In three cases, exactly 50 % of clinicians selected the same module as their first choice.
Only for one target did the first-choice module fall short of a simple majority, with 45.46 %.
Regarding the second-choice selections, the criterion of a simple majority was met for 46.84 % of the 23 targets.

Agreement in percent for both the second as well as the first rating and majority outcomes for both the first and second ratings are provided online on OSF (link will be provided after peer-review to retain anonymity).

In all four instances (first rating -first choice, first rating -second choice, second rating -first choice, second rating -second choice), the Gibbs-Martin Index was 0.5, indicating a moderate consensus among clinicians across items, with some preference patterns emerging alongside notable distributional spread.
Accordingly, no differences from the first to the second rating and between first and second choices in the variability of clinicians' recommendations could be detected.
Regarding the mean agreement rating of > 5 on a 7-point scale, all first-choice modules met this threshold.

Regarding the primary criterion of this focus group -namely, a majority agreement (i. e. > 2) -the criterion was met for 31 out of 46 target-module matches (67.40 %). 22 targetmodule matches received unanimous agreement from all science experts.

text.text: Figure 2 illustrates the frequency with which the nine CBT modules were selected as first or second choices in the clinicians' rating after discussion in phase 1.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">2</ref> illustrates the frequency with which the nine CBT modules were selected as first or second choices in the clinicians' rating after discussion in phase 1.

text.text: It is noteworthy that "third-wave" modules such as Self-Compassion, Acceptance, and Values were selected considerably more frequently than "classical" CBT modules like Attentional Control or Relaxation.

This trend was also explicitly noted by several clinicians, who reported choosing "third-wave" modules more frequently in the study context than they typically do in routine clinical practice, where Attentional Control and Relaxation are more commonly applied.
Notably, all nine modules were selected at least once, suggesting the overall clinical relevance and perceived applicability of the pre-selected module pool.
Note.
Red bars = first choice, blue bars = second choice.

Bars represent the absolute number with which the modules were selected as first or second choice across all targets by all clinical experts (22 experts recommended 23 first and second choices each, resulting in 506 first and 506 second choices).
This figure was created in R Studio.
Another noteworthy observation concerns changes in agreement in the clinicians' recommendations before and after the discussion in phase 1.
These two ratings can themselves be interpreted as separate rounds, with the second rating reflecting a more informed decision following group discussion.
For the first-choice modules, agreement increased in 18 instances and remained unchanged in two.
In three instances, agreement decreased from the first to the second rating.
Overall, the agreement regarding the first-choice modules increased from 56.72 % before to 66.40 % after discussion.
For the second-choice modules, agreement increased after group discussion for 18 targets and remained unchanged in three instances.
In two instances, agreement decreased from the first to the second rating.
Overall, agreement regarding the second-choice modules increased from 38.34 % before to 46.84 % after group discussion.
Agreement percentages from the first and second rating are provided online (link will be provided after peer-review to retain anonymity).
In qualitative research, anticipating the point of data saturation is crucial for planning the number of rounds, focus groups, and overall sample size.
In this study, module choices were descriptively summarised based on the most frequently selected options after each group of phase 1 (link will be provided after peer-review to retain anonymity).
For eight out of 23 items, both the first-and second-choice modules were already clearly established following the first focus group.
For an additional five targets, the first-choice module (but not the second-choice) was determined after the first group.
Only one item showed a change after the fifth focus group, resulting in a tie.

Overall, this descriptive analysis suggests that for the majority of items, module preferences were established within the first one to three focus group sessions, with only minor changes occurring during the final two groups.

text.text: Of all 46 target-module matches, 21 (46.65 %) fulfilled all three primary criteria: a majority of clinicians in phase 1, a mean agreement of > 5 in phase 2, and a majority of science experts in phase 3.

text.text: For an additional 17 matches (36.96 %), at least one majority -either among clinicians or science experts -was present, and these matches were therefore also included in the final matrix.
Of these 17 matches, there were two that were included despite missing two criteria.
The remaining eight target-module matches (17.39 %), all of which involved second-choice modules, were subject to discussion within the study team.
These were selected based on the frequency of module selections in phase 1 and the qualitative comments from both phases 2 and 3.
A detailed summary of the final Matching Matrix, including the fulfilment of each phase criterion and the rationale for decision on the eight discussed items is provided in the Appendix (D).
