The aim of this mixed-methods study was to develop a structured Matching Matrix linking two CBT modules to individual, chronic pain-related processes, thereby addressing a central challenge in personalised psychotherapy: how to support clinical decision-making in the absence of robust, component-level empirical data.
Using a group Delphi approach with clinicians and a focus group with science experts, a complete matrix covering 23 target processes was generated.
Notably, first-choice module selections showed high robustness, as all first-choice selections met the predefined criteria and required no further discussion by the study team.
This suggests that clinicians and science experts share a substantial degree of implicit agreement regarding core intervention-target relationships in chronic pain treatment.

On the other hand, there were two module recommendations included in the final Matching Matrix that missed two of the three predefined criteria, and no recommendation reached unanimous agreement, potentially reflecting remaining discrepancies in the experts' clinical reasoning.
Eight of the 23 second-choice modules required additional discussion within the study team, as they did not meet the obligatory criteria.
This may reflect the broader framing of second-choice modules as "alternatives", potentially encouraging clinicians to consider a wider range of options and thereby reducing consensus.

These findings support the idea that there may be multiple viable intervention strategies for addressing a given target process (Scheidegger et al., 2023), reinforcing the idea that personalised treatment should accommodate flexibility rather than enforce singular solutions.
text.formatted: These findings support the idea that there may be multiple viable intervention strategies for addressing a given target process <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Scheidegger et al., 2023)</ref>, reinforcing the idea that personalised treatment should accommodate flexibility rather than enforce singular solutions.

text.text: Across both science experts and clinician groups, "third-wave" CBT modules (e. g.
Self-Compassion, Acceptance) were more frequently selected and received higher agreement.
This may reflect their perceived relevance for chronic pain, where acceptance-based and contextual approaches are widely regarded as particularly suitable.
At the same time, this tendency could reflect cognitive biases -such as availability or recency effects due to recent training experiences.

Conformity effects seem unlikely to have primarily contributed to the preferential selection of third-wave modules, as these modules were also selected most frequently by clinicians in the initial independent rating in Phase 1 (see Appendix E).
In the case of science experts, this may in part be explained by selection bias, as two of the four participants reported specific expertise in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy.

Overall, our findings cannot determine whether the greater emphasis on third-wave modules reflects a bias in expert judgment or the composition of the sample or a genuine perception that these modules are particularly relevant for the psychological processes assessed.
The present design was not intended to distinguish between these explanations.
A more systematic documentation of the arguments underlying module selection would have allowed for a deeper examination of these influences and represents an important direction for future research.

Additionally, investigating possible differences in clinical decision-making between therapists in training and licensed psychotherapists or even between male and female clinicians presents another step for future research.

In conclusion, replication with larger and more representative samples of clinicians (e.g. from community-based settings) and researchers could help determine the robustness of the pattern found in this study and clarify the extent to which it reflects expertise, sample composition, or systematic biases in treatment recommendations.
Interestingly, various modules were selected for items of the same process.

This observation supports the notion that discernible facets of the same process may require different treatment approaches, and that using for example sum scores of processes assessed with multiple items might result in loss of therapy-relevant information (Pena Loray et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This observation supports the notion that discernible facets of the same process may require different treatment approaches, and that using for example sum scores of processes assessed with multiple items might result in loss of therapy-relevant information <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Pena Loray et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, these results echo ongoing debates regarding mechanisms of change in psychotherapy.

A central assumption underlying the present Matching Matrix, as well as previous attempts to develop matching matrices or algorithmic decision-tools (cf. Fernandez et al., 2017), is that a given intervention can be matched to a specific treatment target.
text.formatted: A central assumption underlying the present Matching Matrix, as well as previous attempts to develop matching matrices or algorithmic decision-tools (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Fernandez et al., 2017)</ref>, is that a given intervention can be matched to a specific treatment target.

text.text: However, it seems unlikely that specific interventions only affect one target at a time (Eronen, 2020; Henry et al., 2022), just as different treatment modules may influence the same target or outcome (Scheidegger et al., 2023).
text.formatted: However, it seems unlikely that specific interventions only affect one target at a time <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Eronen, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Henry et al., 2022)</ref>, just as different treatment modules may influence the same target or outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Scheidegger et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This is consistent with research comparing different treatment approaches (e.g., Zgierska et al., 2025), as well as with the present finding that clinical experts did not consistently recommend the same two modules for a given target.
text.formatted: This is consistent with research comparing different treatment approaches (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Zgierska et al., 2025)</ref>, as well as with the present finding that clinical experts did not consistently recommend the same two modules for a given target.

text.text: Moreover, emerging evidence questions the existence of strictly intervention-specific mechanisms (Burns, 2025), suggesting that selecting modules for isolated targets may be overly simplistic.
text.formatted: Moreover, emerging evidence questions the existence of strictly intervention-specific mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Burns, 2025)</ref>, suggesting that selecting modules for isolated targets may be overly simplistic.

text.text: Nevertheless, identifying a primary treatment target may remain clinically useful.

In practice, selecting an intervention based on the process facet considered most relevant to a patient's current difficulties provides a feasible starting point for treatment planning, even if or even because the selected intervention is likely to affect additional process facets.
Understanding the differential effects of theoretically distinct interventions thus remains a key challenge for improving CBT (Cohen et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Understanding the differential effects of theoretically distinct interventions thus remains a key challenge for improving CBT <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Cohen et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Accounting systematically for interconnected effects would require moving beyond a one-to-one matching approach.
Future work may therefore benefit from identifying efficacy profiles that capture patterns of effects across multiple interacting targets.
Such analyses may become increasingly feasible as larger datasets linking interventions, psychological processes, and treatment outcomes become available.
Until then, expert-based matching provides a pragmatic approach to structuring clinical decision-making in the absence of sufficient empirical data.
At the same time, identified moderators are likely unspecific to the treatment form (Chen et al., 2023).
text.formatted: At the same time, identified moderators are likely unspecific to the treatment form <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Chen et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, the treatment strategy might be less relevant for the outcome than nonspecific treatment mechanisms, highlighting the need to investigate both intervention-specific and common mechanisms in personalised CBT.
Data saturation within the clinician sample may have been reached prior to the fifth clinician group.
From a resource-oriented perspective, fewer groups could therefore be sufficient for developing a Matching Matrix of this kind.
The focus group of science experts proved to be useful for validating the clinicians' selections, with 17 of the final target-module matches being supported by at least one majority criterion.
In most cases, agreement between clinicians in phase 1 increased from first to second rating.

This might reflect a tendency to agree with the previous focus group, the results of which were presented after the first rating, enhanced by the prompt to deliver arguments in favour with these recommendations.
Cases in which agreement decreased could be explained by especially empathetically made arguments against the previous results that did not occur very often.
The fact that agreement also decreased in some instances implicates that clinicians did not uniformly adopt the recommendations of previous groups or of one another.
However, these explanations are based on the impression of the conducting researcher (first author) and cannot definitely be determined due to the lack of recordings of Phase 1.
Future research should consider transcribing the arguments provided so that agreement shifts can be analysed more systematically.
From a clinical perspective, personalised psychotherapy rarely involves a single intervention in isolation.
Rather, treatment decisions unfold iteratively, requiring clinicians to determine not only which, but also when to apply an intervention (Fisher & Boswell, 2016).
text.formatted: Rather, treatment decisions unfold iteratively, requiring clinicians to determine not only which, but also when to apply an intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Fisher & Boswell, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This study adhered to current recommendations for systematic and structured clinician surveys (Kaiser & Roth, 2022), employing a collaborative framework to enhance the acceptability of the resulting matrix (Levinson et al., 2024) as well as its ecological validity, and predefining methodological procedures in accordance with established guidelines (Diamond et al., 2014; Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015).
text.formatted: This study adhered to current recommendations for systematic and structured clinician surveys <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Kaiser & Roth, 2022)</ref>, employing a collaborative framework to enhance the acceptability of the resulting matrix <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Levinson et al., 2024)</ref> as well as its ecological validity, and predefining methodological procedures in accordance with established guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Diamond et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Trevelyan & Robinson, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In response to common criticisms of Delphi studies, indicators of clinical expertise were assessed following relevant recommendations (Baker et al., 2006; Boulkedid et al., 2011; Hill et al., 2017; Overholser, 2010) and transparently reported alongside consensus in the form of percentage agreement (Diamond et al., 2014).
text.formatted: In response to common criticisms of Delphi studies, indicators of clinical expertise were assessed following relevant recommendations <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baker et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Boulkedid et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Hill et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Overholser, 2010)</ref> and transparently reported alongside consensus in the form of percentage agreement <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Diamond et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: A further strength of the present study lies in the composition of the expert samples.
The literature recommends heterogenous samples involving experts from diverse professional backgrounds and settings (J. Baker et al., 2006).
text.formatted: The literature recommends heterogenous samples involving experts from diverse professional backgrounds and settings (J. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Baker et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, such an approach reflects the multimodal treatment reality of chronic pain.
In this study, a minimum level of expertise was ensured, while still allowing for a broad range of professional roles and clinical experience.
As such, we consider the clinician sample to be well suited to the study objective, with the results likely to be both ecologically valid and reasonably reliable.
The inclusion of psychological science experts complemented the clinician perspective by introducing a more theoretical and research-informed viewpoint.
Taken together, these two expert groups may contribute to bridging the science-practice gap -an effect that could be amplified by bringing science experts and clinicians into direct discussion.
Additionally, both the number of focus groups (Vogt et al., 2004) and the sample sizes in the Delphi rounds (J. Baker et al., 2006) followed established methodological recommendations.
text.formatted: Additionally, both the number of focus groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Vogt et al., 2004)</ref> and the sample sizes in the Delphi rounds (J. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Baker et al., 2006)</ref> followed established methodological recommendations.

text.text: From an epistemic perspective, the present study should be understood as an interim step between intuitive clinical judgement and fully data-driven decision-support systems.
It reflects clinician and researcher recommendations in the sense of a hypothesis-generating framework warranting empirical evaluation.

While previous research suggests a likely mismatch between clinical judgement and data-oriented decision-making tools (Fernandez et al., 2017), collaboration with clinicians appears to be a necessary interim step to generate robust data for algorithmic approaches.
text.formatted: While previous research suggests a likely mismatch between clinical judgement and data-oriented decision-making tools <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fernandez et al., 2017)</ref>, collaboration with clinicians appears to be a necessary interim step to generate robust data for algorithmic approaches.

text.text: The method used to create the present Matching Matrix is replicable, and applying the Matching Matrix in psychotherapy research will allow studying module-specific effects on clearly defined treatment targets.
However, patients have not been included in this study project, which should be considered in future studies.

It is yet unclear how algorithmic decision guidelines such as this Matching Matrix can be incorporated in an interactive, shared-decision making process (Wester et al., 2025), that is and should be the gold-standard in clinical practice.
text.formatted: It is yet unclear how algorithmic decision guidelines such as this Matching Matrix can be incorporated in an interactive, shared-decision making process <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Wester et al., 2025)</ref>, that is and should be the gold-standard in clinical practice.

text.text: Especially as long as evidence for algorithmic decision-tools is scarce, additional information such as patients' preferences should be included (Wester et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Especially as long as evidence for algorithmic decision-tools is scarce, additional information such as patients' preferences should be included <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Wester et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In this study, such additional information was considered regarding contraindications for certain interventions and were discussed in the researcher focus group.
We advise users of the Matching Matrix to reflect if any adverse effects are anticipated when following the recommendations for any individual patient, and of course to obtain informed consent.
The use of a predefined pool of CBT modules introduced a top-down element to the procedure, potentially omitting relevant interventions (e. g. problem-solving).
The same holds true for the predefined set of process items.
However, earlier, unpublished study projects had shown that, in the absence of a predefined module pool, discussions became overly broad and unmanageable within the given timeframe.
Future research should review and extend the predefined pool of CBT modules with other important treatment strategies for chronic pain such as sleep hygiene, problem solving, or communication skills.

It should also consider further strategies to select treatment targets, for example Perceived Causal Networks (Klintwall et al., 2021; Vogel et al., 2025) Additionally, the limit of two modules per target was chosen given the timely constraints of the selection process and with the goal of providing a concise recommendation for clinical practice.
text.formatted: It should also consider further strategies to select treatment targets, for example Perceived Causal Networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Klintwall et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Vogel et al., 2025)</ref> Additionally, the limit of two modules per target was chosen given the timely constraints of the selection process and with the goal of providing a concise recommendation for clinical practice.

text.text: Alternative to selecting only two treatment modules per target, all predefined modules could be ranked for each given target, resulting in a priority evaluation for each target-module match.
Some clinicians reported potential framing effects or the tendency to project personal clinical experience onto the items, since they were presented without contextual case vignettes.

One promising alternative to mitigate this limitation could be to reverse the selection logic -asking clinicians to identify the most relevant target processes for specific modules, rather than selecting modules for processes.
Another possibility would be the use of personas to guide the discussion process (Bartels et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Another possibility would be the use of personas to guide the discussion process <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bartels et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Such personas or case vignettes could also account for different contexts, goals, individual illness beliefs, and also comorbidities and according treatments.
From a methodological perspective, potential order effects cannot be ruled out, as randomisation of item presentation was not feasible.
Future studies should consider randomising the order of items or modules.
Moreover, due to time limitations, the discussions among clinicians and science experts were relatively brief and should be regarded as thought prompts rather than in-depth deliberations.
The sequential design of Phase 1 may have introduced conformity effects and reduced the independence of recommendations.

However, these effects were likely limited due to the independent, anonymous first rating and explicit encouragements to discuss arguments against the emerging group recommendation prior to the second rating.
The results indicated decreasing agreement from the first to the second rating in few instances, suggesting that recommendations were not uniformly influenced by preceding group decisions.
Future research could investigate differences between first and second ratings more systematically, including whether such changes are associated with differential treatment effectiveness.
Recent methodological recommendations for Delphi studies commonly suggest conducting three rounds and using a consensus threshold of at least 80 % in the final round (Hohmann et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent methodological recommendations for Delphi studies commonly suggest conducting three rounds and using a consensus threshold of at least 80 % in the final round <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Hohmann et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, the number of rounds was a prior limited to two, and the agreement thresholds applied in Phases 1 and 3 were below this recommended level.

Given the hypothesis-generating aim of this study, the heterogeneous composition of the clinician sample, and the fact that three complementary selection criteria were applied across the different phases, the liberal agreement thresholds appear justified and still allow to build upon the results for future research.

Nevertheless, future research should consider replicating the present findings using a third Delphi round and more stringent consensus criteria to examine the stability and robustness of the identified matches.
Since no transcripts of the focus groups in phase 1 were made, more detailed insights regarding agreement and disagreement of the clinicians cannot be reported.
The option to leave comments in phase 2 was used by few clinicians as well.
Future research should incorporate a more systematic assessment and analysis of qualitative data.
Additionally, allowing more extensive discussions in future work may facilitate clearer consensus-building and potentially lead to greater convergence among participants.

In the present study, a mixed methods approach including Delphi technique and focus groups was applied in close collaboration with practicing clinicians as well as renowned pain science experts that resulted in a matrix linking CBT modules of first and second choice to 23 chronic pain processes.

By formalising intervention-target relationships, the present Matching Matrix addresses a central bottleneck in personalised psychotherapy: the absence of structured guidance when empirical evidence is incomplete.

The procedure used to develop this Matching Matrix is replicable, suitable to bridge the science-practice gap, and can guide future efforts to personalise psychotherapy, also beyond the context of chronic pain.

Several key questions remain to be answered, including which processes are most suitable as therapeutic targets, how they can best be assessed, and which interventions are most effective in addressing them.

Ultimately, the aim of research in this area should not be to replace clinicians, but to support them in making evidence-based, personalised decisions (Levinson et al., 2024; Lutz et al., 2022; Wester et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Ultimately, the aim of research in this area should not be to replace clinicians, but to support them in making evidence-based, personalised decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Levinson et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Lutz et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Wester et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present study may serve as an interim step towards a more data-based clinical decision process.

A stronger empirical basis is urgently needed to predict the effects of particular methods on defined target processes (Cohen et al., 2023; Murillo et al., 2022) and to determine the usefulness of specific targets versus more complex efficacy profiles in the absence of intervention-specific mechanisms of action (Burns, 2025).

Although the present Matching Matrix does not prescribe a fixed intervention sequence, it is compatible with such an iterative approach by supporting repeated target selection and module assignment across treatment phases.

Future research should examine how such matrices can be integrated into longitudinal treatment planning, including the determination of meaningful endpoints of the intervention and the treatment in general.

In clinical practice, application of this matching matrix would encompass identifying a treatment target, e.g. using the ProCEss item set (V. E.Hofmann, Glombiewski, Heider, et al., 2026a; V. E. Hofmann, Glombiewski, Prasch, et al., 2026), and using the Matching Matrix as guidance for treatment mapping.

text.text: However, since the actual efficacy of the Matching Matrix has not yet been evaluated, we do not recommend relying on the Matching Matrix alone in routine clinical practice.While the present matrix does not replace empirical effect estimates, it provides a formalised representation of expert knowledge that can serve as a foundation for future datadriven refinement.

Importantly, the challenge of evidence-based personalisation in the absence of sufficient empirical data is not unique to chronic pain, but reflects a broader issue in psychotherapy research, where the aspiration for personalised treatment often outpaces the available evidence base.

Consequently, both the Matching Matrix itself as well as the detailed description of the development process present valuable starting points for future research on personalised CBT within and beyond the context of chronic pain.
With growing evidence on the effects of specific interventions, clinical decision-support tools may become increasingly data-driven, complementing rather than replacing clinical judgement.

Advances in artificial intelligence may further enhance such tools by facilitating the integration of complex evidence into treatment recommendations or identifying efficacy profiles beyond simple intervention-target matches.

Such tools might also include whether patients receive multiple (multimodal) treatments, possibly in different settings by different practitioners, at the same time and how they can best be coordinated.
research can build on this Matching Matrix to investigate the effects of individualised intervention selection and to further evaluate whether process-based matching improves treatment outcomes.

Moreover, the procedure described in this study may provide a framework for developing personalised treatment recommendations in other areas where empirical evidence for specific treatments is currently limited.

Until sufficient data is available to support data-driven algorithms, larger samples of clinical and scientific experts may further strengthen the robustness of the Matching Matrix and enable subgroup analyses.
Such analyses could provide further insights into clinical reasoning across different professional backgrounds and levels of expertise.
